item.title: Geometric Kernel Diversity: An Axiomatic Diversity Measure in Euclidean Space
item.description: arXiv:2610.19570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying the diversity of a set of objects is a fundamental problem in machine learning and statistics. Mironov and Prokhorenkova (2025) recently showed that three axioms-monotonicity, uniqueness, and continuity-are crucial for a reliable diversity measure and that none of the standard metrics in the literature satisfy all three. They also constructed two measures that do satisfy the axioms, but both are NP-hard to compute, leaving open the question of whether efficient axiomatic diversity measures can exist. We study a Euclidean-restricted version of this question. We introduce Geometric Kernel Diversity (GKD), which associates a radial kernel solid with each point and measures the volume of their union. We show that canonical GKD satisfies all three Mironov-Prokhorenkova axioms on Euclidean-realizable inputs. For canonical GKD, we give exact polynomial-time algorithms in dimensions $d \le 3$. In arbitrary dimensions, we give a randomized algorithm that returns a $(1 \pm \varepsilon)$-approximation with probability at least $1-\delta$ in time $O \left(\frac{nd}{\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{2}{\delta}\right)$ for $n$ points. The axiomatic guarantee applies to exact canonical GKD; the randomized algorithm approximates this deterministic quantity. We further show that the two diversity measures of Mironov and Prokhorenkova (2025) remain NP-hard on Euclidean-realizable inputs and, unless $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{RP}$, admit no FPRAS even on this restricted domain.
item.dc:creator: Ditbul Ban, Younghun Roh, Julian Shun, Vihan Lakshman

item.title: Towards Learning-Guided Discovery of Extremal Geometric Constructions: A PatternBoost Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.19980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extremal constructions play a central role in the design and analysis of algorithms. Integrality-gap instances expose the limitations of relaxations, while hard configurations reveal structural sources of computational difficulty. Such constructions, however, are still typically discovered through a slow, manual process. This paper investigates how machine learning can accelerate their discovery to support algorithm design and analysis. We build on PatternBoost, a framework alternating local search with generation from a trained transformer, using its Axplorer implementation to investigate three problems: integrality gaps for maximum independent set of rectangles, integrality gaps for stabbing unit squares with axis-parallel lines, and hard instances for recursive guillotine cutting. By exploring candidate representations, local search operations, and surrogate models used to rank candidates before exact verification, we carefully adapt the framework to these combinatorial geometry problems.While naive representations and search strategies fail to find non-trivial instances, our tailored adaptation discovers numerous non-trivial constructions. For stabbing unit squares, the method reaches a gap of $20/13\approx 1.54$, improving on the literature's best known lower bound of $3/2$. Purely automated search converges rapidly and then plateaus, prompting the question of what is required to push the bound higher still. We find that initial instance diversity plays an important role: with modest expert input via a structured staircase construction, the system reaches an improved integrality gap of $14/9\approx 1.555$. These results demonstrate that machine learning and domain expertise can be combined to discover new extremal constructions that advance algorithmic lower bounds.
item.dc:creator: Deepak Ajwani, Paula Carroll, Rishikesh Gajjala, Ananta Manoranjan, Ryan O'Connor, Rajiv Raman, Saurabh Ray, Aimen Taha

item.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
item.description: arXiv:2610.20244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity. Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function. We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective. Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$. The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots. Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.
item.dc:creator: Sayan Bandyapadhyay, William Lochet, Saket Saurabh, Jie Xue

item.title: Arithmetic Visibility in Polygons: Curved Sight in the Art Gallery
item.description: arXiv:2610.19506v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the classical art gallery problem, a guard sees a target when the segment joining them lies entirely within the polygon. We explore what changes when sight may bend along regular arcs on absolutely irreducible curves, but only those defined by primitive integer polynomials of total degree at most \(d\) and coefficient height at most \(H\). We call such curves admissible sight carriers. Arcs can dramatically improve sight. In a one-sided comb, no straight-line guard sees selected targets in two different teeth, yet a single central guard sees a chosen target in every tooth along parabolic carriers. Sight can also fail in two different ways. Geometrically, the polygon may block every sight arc of the allowed degree between two points. For instance, in an alternating comb, the number of guards needed for a row of targets spanning the comb grows linearly with the number of sides at each fixed degree, even for carriers with arbitrary real coefficients. Arithmetically, no admissible carrier may pass through the points at all. Even in the unit square, at fixed \(d\) and \(H\), the proportion of rational targets that must guard themselves tends to one as the height bound grows. An algebraic target may lie on no rational curve of degree at most \(d\), however large \(H\) is. Both failures can be overcome for finite target sets by allowing the degree and coefficient height to grow. We show that every finite set of algebraic targets in a rational polygon becomes visible from any rational interior guard, with explicit bounds. We also construct, for every \(d\), arbitrarily large Galois orbits in the unit square, all of projective height \(4^{d+1}\), whose points must each guard themselves at degree \(d\) for every \(H\). Yet at degree \(d+1\) and coefficient height one, a single guard sees the whole orbit along \(Z(Y-X^{d+1})\).
item.dc:creator: Malik Barrett

item.title: Structural identification in general crystalline systems via Voronoi cell topology
item.description: arXiv:2610.20498v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Widely used methods for identifying crystal structure in atomistic simulations are limited in practice to a handful of simple structures, leaving many important crystalline systems without automated classification techniques. Voronoi topology analysis offers a route to classifying arbitrary crystalline and defect environments, but realizing this potential first requires enumerating the Voronoi cell topologies that can arise under thermal perturbation of a structure of interest. We present an algorithm that deterministically enumerates all Voronoi cell topologies arising from generic infinitesimal perturbations of an arbitrary crystal structure, producing structural classifiers that extend automated identification to general crystalline systems. We demonstrate the approach on several structures of general interest.
item.dc:creator: Emanuel A. Lazar, Chris H. Rycroft
